draft.title: Supporting a reading with evidence
card: Evidence is a short, precise quotation or reference taken from the text. Choose the few words that matter, not a whole passage.
Weave the quotation into your own sentence, so your argument stays in charge.
After the evidence, explain how it supports your point. Name a word, technique or detail and say what it suggests.
Evidence without analysis does not prove anything. A quotation on its own leaves the reader to guess your point.
draft.remember: Pick short evidence, then explain how it proves your point.

a.q: Which choice makes a quotation actually support an argument?
opts: Explaining what its words suggest about the point
Placing it on its own line after the point
Making it as long as possible
Repeating it in the next sentence
a.why: A quotation supports an argument when you explain how its words prove your point. Length or repetition adds nothing, and a quotation left alone is still unexplained.

b.q: Jess argues that a narrator feels lonely. She writes: The narrator eats alone by the window. What is missing from her paragraph?
opts: An explanation of how this detail shows loneliness
A longer quotation from the same page
A summary of the whole story
b.why: Jess gives a detail from the text but does not say how it shows loneliness. Evidence needs analysis to prove a point. More quotation would still leave it unexplained.
b.clue: She has the evidence, but what has she not done with it?

a.best: Explaining what its words suggest about the point

b.best: An explanation of how this detail shows loneliness
